# Fernhill Tea: three agents fix the checkout

Example data for thimble's tour. Fernhill Tea is a made-up online tea shop. Every agent, message and line of code
here is made up.

Customers said the checkout charged the wrong total for an order with a gift box. Three Claude Code agents shared the
work and talked on a message board:

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `agents/agent-1.jsonl` | the agent that found the bug and fixed it |
| `agents/agent-2.jsonl` | the agent that wrote a test for it |
| `agents/agent-3.jsonl` | the agent that reviewed the fix |
| `board.jsonl` | the messages the agents sent each other |
| `shop/checkout.py` | the checkout's code after the fix |

The bug: the checkout added the gift box fee before it took the member discount off, so members also got 10% off
the fee.

checks.name: Heads up
checks.prompt:
A heads-up marks words of the answer for a detail that the analyst should know before they rely on the answer. The analyst reads it in a small box beside the answer, apart from the sentence that holds its words. A heads-up only informs. It says what the detail changes in the analyst's understanding of the answer, and the analyst decides what to do about it.

- Give a heads-up only when the analyst would understand the answer differently if they missed the detail.
- Look for such a detail in every answer. Give at most one heads-up per answer, for the detail that would change their understanding the most.
- Such details are often in the cards and in what the session read for the answer. Look for a claim that says more than its records hold, a number whose records come from another period, group or scope than its words say, or a drawing that disagrees with the words.
- Name the detail itself, for example "the 412 counts all 14 months, and March alone is 37". Do not remark on how someone reasoned.

A heads-up is one add_comment on the sentence that holds the detail. Its text names the detail and what it means for the answer. Its details give the evidence. A document counts as one answer.

checks.name: Explainers
checks.prompt:
An explainer marks words of the answer. It gives the background that a reader new to the records needs to see what those words mean for the claim. The analyst reads it in a small box beside the answer, then reads on. So an explainer is short: a sentence or two on what the words mean, and one line on where they mattered.

Words can need an explainer whether or not they are familiar. Words need none when the answer already gives their background, or when the analyst already has it. Early in a session the analyst has little of this background. Later, they have most of it.

An explainer is one add_comment on the sentence that holds the term. Its text names the term exactly as the analyst reads it. Then the text says what the term means, for a reader new to the field. Its details say where the term mattered in this work.

checks.name: Judgment calls
checks.prompt: Comment only on a sentence that presents the writer's judgment or interpretation as if the data showed it. Even then, comment only when a reader who took the sentence as fact could reach a wrong conclusion.
